result: Egr2-positive BC cell derivatives migrate along spinal nerves to the skin between E11.5 and E15.5, progressively detach from nerves, and integrate into the vascular plexus. The proportion of traced cells in contact with nerves decreases from 89.9% at E12.5 to 9.4% at E15.5, while those in contact with blood vessels increase from 10.1% to 90.6% over the same period.
evaluation: Claims C5-C29 collectively provide strong temporal and spatial evidence for BC cell migration and detachment. The quantitative data (C24-C26) showing the shift from nerve-associated to vessel-associated cells is well-documented in Figure 1M with appropriate statistical analysis. The microscopy images (C9-C13) provide visual confirmation of the migration pattern, and the inference of migration (C14) is well-supported by the temporal progression data.

result: Multiple complementary approaches (in situ hybridization, RT-PCR, RNAscope, and scRNA-seq) confirm the absence of de novo Egr2 expression in traced cells outside of BC cells at E12.5, validating that Tom-positive cells originate exclusively from Egr2-expressing BC cells.
evaluation: Claims C17-C21 provide multiple independent lines of evidence using different methodologies to exclude ectopic Cre expression. The convergence of results from in situ hybridization (C17), RT-PCR (C18), RNAscope (C19), and scRNA-seq (C20) provides strong support for the conclusion (C21). This is critical for validating the lineage tracing approach.

result: Egr2-traced BC cell derivatives behave differently from Prss56-traced BC cells, with Egr2-traced cells detaching from nerves and integrating into vasculature while Prss56-traced cells remain nerve-associated. Egr2 inactivation does not affect this vascular integration.
evaluation: Claims C30-C33 are supported by comparative data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 showing distinct behaviors between Egr2 and Prss56 lineages. The lack of phenotype in Egr2 mutants (C32) is demonstrated by comparison of mutant and control embryos. This establishes functional heterogeneity within BC populations and rules out a cell-autonomous role for Egr2 in MC differentiation.

result: Traced BC cell derivatives in the skin vasculature express multiple MC markers (ABCC9, NG2, PDGFRβ, SMA) and exhibit morphologies consistent with pericytes and vSMCs. These cells constitute approximately 68% of NG2-positive MCs at E15.5 and 66% at P1, and persist through P30.
evaluation: Claims C34-C41 provide comprehensive characterization of MC identity through morphology (C34-C35), marker expression (C36), and quantification (C37-C38). The data are well-documented in Figure 2 with appropriate statistical analysis. The persistence through P30 (C39, C41) demonstrates long-term maintenance of this population. The quantification is robust with clear methodology described.

result: At E12.5, ventral root BC-derived cells include both Sox10-positive and Sox10-negative populations, with the Sox10-negative cells expressing mesenchymal markers (Tbx18, Col1a1, Pdgfra). These Sox10-negative cells migrate along nerves to the skin and differentiate into MCs, while Sox10-negative cells are absent from dorsal roots.
evaluation: Claims C42-C53 establish early specification of MC fate through multiple approaches including immunolabeling (C42-C45), RNAscope (C48-C50), and comparison between dorsal and ventral roots (C46-C47). The expression of mesenchymal markers in Tom-positive cells (C48-C50) is clearly shown in Figure 3I-N. The dorsal/ventral difference (C46, C53) provides important spatial specificity, though C46 relies on data not shown which is a limitation.

result: Ventral root Egr2-expressing BC cells have dual embryonic origins: neural crest (NC) and Tbx18-expressing pial cells. Lineage tracing with NC markers (Wnt1Cre, Sox10Cre-Ert2) and neural tube markers (Olig2Cre) shows no contribution to skin MCs, while Tbx18Cre-ERT2 tracing reveals Sox10-negative cells that attach to ventral roots and give rise to MCs.
evaluation: Claims C54-C66 establish dual origins through negative results from NC/neural tube tracing (C58-C59) and positive results from Tbx18 tracing (C62-C64). The Tbx18 expression pattern at E9.5 (C61) is consistent with cited literature. The conclusion of dual origins (C65) is well-supported by the combination of negative and positive lineage tracing results. However, C66 is more speculative as it proposes a model without direct evidence for Egr2 activation timing.

result: Single-cell RNA sequencing of 2209 Tom-positive cells from E12.5 skin reveals three main populations: Schwann cell precursors (47%), mesenchymal progenitors (48%), and mature mural cells (6%). The MP population expresses mesenchymal markers (Pdgfra, Pdgfrb, Tbx18, Col1a1) despite most cells being nerve-attached, and includes a chondroprogenitor subpopulation (MP5).
evaluation: Claims C67-C84 provide comprehensive scRNA-seq analysis with appropriate quality metrics (C68) and validation (C69). The identification of three main populations (C71-C75) is well-supported by marker expression patterns shown in Figure 5. The finding that 54% of cells show mesenchymal signature despite 90% being nerve-attached (C74) is particularly important for supporting early specification. The identification of chondroprogenitors (C81-C82) is interesting but more speculative. The integration with immunolabeling data (C83) strengthens the overall conclusions.

result: Egr2-traced MCs are found in serous membranes (pretracheal fasciae, pericardium, peritoneum) of adult mice but not in internal organs. These MCs are interspersed with non-traced MCs, suggesting multiple embryonic origins for serous membrane MCs.
evaluation: Claims C85-C92 document the presence of Egr2-traced MCs in serous membranes (C87) but acknowledge significant limitations. The authors explicitly state it remains unclear whether these derive from BC cells (C91) due to lack of data on earlier Egr2 expression. The sample size is limited (n=2 adult mice, C87-C88), and the connection to BC cells is speculative (C92). While the observations are valid, the interpretation regarding BC contribution is uncertain.

result: Genetic ablation of Egr2-expressing cells causes embryonic lethality around E15.5 and results in significant depletion of NG2-positive MCs in skin (from 17.9% to 6.5% coverage) without affecting nerve development. Myeloid-derived MCs cannot fully compensate for the loss.
evaluation: Claims C93-C103 provide functional validation through genetic ablation. The quantification of MC depletion (C98) is statistically significant and well-documented in Figure 6H. The lack of effect on nerve development (C99-C100) is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1. However, there are important caveats: incomplete penetrance (C95), small sample size for complete ablation (n=4 mutants, n=3 controls), and uncertainty about the cause of lethality (C103) since ablation affects all Egr2-positive cells, not just BC cells.

result: The study establishes that mouse skin MCs have dual embryonic origins: approximately one-third from myeloid precursors and two-thirds from Egr2-expressing ventral BC cells. BC-derived MCs originate from Sox10-negative, pia matter-derived cells that migrate along nerves before detaching and differentiating into pericytes and vSMCs.
evaluation: Claims C105-C114 provide a comprehensive summary of the major findings. The quantification of BC contribution (C106) is well-supported by data in Figure 2E-G. The distinction between Sox10-positive SCP-fated cells (C109) and Sox10-negative MC-fated cells (C110) is supported by multiple lines of evidence. The functional importance is demonstrated by ablation studies (C111). The broader implications for serous membranes (C112-C113) are more speculative but reasonable given the data.

result: Ventral root BC cells comprise two functionally distinct populations: Sox10-positive cells that become SCPs and Sox10-negative cells expressing mesenchymal markers that become MCs. Both BC-derived and myeloid-derived MCs show discontinuous distribution along vessels, suggesting a common vascular recruitment mechanism.
evaluation: Claims C115-C123 synthesize multiple observations into a coherent model. The distinction between dorsal and ventral root BC populations (C115-C116) is well-supported. The identification of Sox10-negative mesenchymal cells (C117) is documented by immunolabeling and RNAscope. The scRNA-seq data (C118) provides molecular support. The comparison with myeloid-derived MCs (C119-C120) is based on cited work and current observations. However, the proposed attraction mechanism (C121-C122) is speculative and not directly tested.

result: BC cells exhibit functional heterogeneity with early fate specification. Egr2 and Prss56 mark partially overlapping but functionally distinct BC subpopulations. Tbx18-expressing cells attach to ventral roots before E11.5 without expressing Sox10, likely contributing to the MC-producing BC subpopulation that originates from meningeal fibroblast precursors rather than neural crest.
evaluation: Claims C124-C134 establish BC heterogeneity and early specification. The lack of Egr2 function in MC differentiation (C124) is supported by mutant analysis. The comparison with Prss56 lineage (C126-C127) is well-documented. The Tbx18 lineage tracing (C129) provides evidence for early specification (C128). The exclusion of NC origin (C133) is supported by negative lineage tracing with multiple drivers. The connection to meningeal fibroblasts (C134) is supported by Tbx18 expression pattern and cited literature.

result: Heterogeneity in BC embryonic origins explains differential lethality phenotypes: NC-specific Egr2 ablation (Wnt1Cre;Egr2GFP/DT) is viable while pan-Egr2 ablation causes embryonic lethality at E15.5, indicating non-overlapping populations are targeted.
evaluation: Claims C135-C138 provide an explanation for differential ablation phenotypes. The molecular heterogeneity within NC-derived BCs (C135) is supported by published and unpublished data. The comparison of ablation phenotypes (C136-C137) integrates current findings with cited work. The inference about non-overlapping populations (C138) is logical given the data, though the exact cause of lethality in pan-Egr2 ablation remains unclear.

result: The study reveals dual embryonic origins (BC-derived and myeloid-derived) for both skin pericytes and vSMCs, with each population unable to fully compensate for the other upon depletion. BC-derived MP clusters show molecular heterogeneity and share markers (Pdgfrα, Col1a1) with CNS MC subtypes involved in fibrosis.
evaluation: Claims C139-C150 place findings in the context of MC heterogeneity literature. The dual origin finding (C144) is well-supported by current data and cited work. The lack of compensation (C145-C147) is demonstrated by ablation studies in both systems. The molecular heterogeneity (C148) is shown by scRNA-seq. The comparison with CNS MC subtypes (C149) is interesting but the functional significance remains unclear (C150). The discussion appropriately acknowledges limitations and open questions.

result: Background information establishes that BC cells form at CNS/PNS interfaces and express Egr2 and/or Prss56 markers. Previous fate mapping with Prss56Cre showed BC derivatives migrate to DRGs and skin, giving rise to Schwann cells, sensory neurons, terminal glia, and melanocytes.
evaluation: Claims C1-C4 provide established background knowledge supported by appropriate citations to previous work (Coulpier et al., 2009; Niederländer and Lumsden, 1996; Gresset et al., 2015; Radomska et al., 2019). These claims accurately represent prior findings and set the context for the current study.

result: About two-thirds of newborn skin MCs originate from Egr2-expressing BC cells.
evaluation: Claim C104 is supported by quantification data in Figure 2E-G showing 68% at E15.5 and 66% at P1, though the text incorrectly references Figure 3F and G. This is a key quantitative finding that establishes the major contribution of BC cells to skin MCs.
